title: Veteran-owned small business certification (VetCert)
summary: Certifying your business as Veteran-owned, or service-disabled Veteran-owned, lets you compete for federal contracts set aside specifically for you. The government targets at least 5 percent of federal contracting dollars at service-disabled Veteran-owned firms.
amount: Access to sole-source and set-aside federal contracts
eligibility: The VA identifies you as a Veteran, or as a service-disabled Veteran for SDVOSB status
At least 51 percent of the business is owned and controlled by one or more Veterans
For SDVOSB, at least 51 percent is owned by service-disabled Veterans
The business meets SBA small business size standards for its industry
A permanently disabled Veteran may still qualify where a spouse or caregiver runs daily operations
details: Certification is handled by the Small Business Administration. Apply through the SBA certifications portal, not through the VA.
Certified Veteran-owned firms can compete under the VA Vets First program as well as government-wide set-asides.
The SBA also runs a Surplus Personal Property program giving access to unused federal property through State Agencies for Surplus Property.
Help line: 866-722-4357, Monday to Friday, 8am to 6pm Eastern.

title: Dependency and Indemnity Compensation (DIC) for survivors
summary: A tax-free monthly payment to the surviving spouse, children, or dependent parents of a service member who died on duty, or of a Veteran who died from a service-connected condition.
amount: Tax-free monthly payment, varying by survivor type and dependents
eligibility: The service member died while on active duty, active duty for training, or inactive-duty training
Or the Veteran died from a service-connected condition
Or the Veteran had a totally disabling service-connected rating for 10 years before death, 5 years after discharge, or 1 year if a former prisoner of war
Surviving spouse: married within 15 years of discharge, or married at least a year, or you had a child together
Surviving children: unmarried, under 18, or under 23 and in school, and not already covered by the spouse payment
Surviving parents: biological, adoptive, or foster, with income below the limit
details: REMARRIAGE RULE, which catches many families out: a surviving spouse who remarries can keep DIC if they were at least 57 at remarriage before December 2003, or at least 55 at remarriage from January 2021 onward.
Rates change every year with a cost-of-living adjustment, so check the current table rather than a figure you were quoted before.
Filing is free. An accredited service officer will help at no charge.

title: Survivors and Dependents Educational Assistance (Chapter 35)
summary: Monthly payments toward education for the children and spouses of a Veteran who is permanently and totally disabled from service, died from a service-connected cause, or is missing, captured, or detained.
amount: Up to 36 months of monthly payments, or 45 months if training began before August 2018
eligibility: The Veteran or service member is permanently and totally disabled from a service-connected condition, died of a service-connected cause, is missing in action, captured, forcibly detained, or hospitalized for a service-connected disability
Children: any age if eligibility began on or after 1 August 2023. Otherwise 18, or younger with a high school diploma or GED
Spouses: eligible whether married or unmarried at the time of application
details: TIME LIMITS depend on when eligibility began. For children eligible on or after 1 August 2023 there is no time limit at all. Before that date it is generally 8 years, ending at age 26.
For spouses, no limit if the qualifying event was on or after 1 August 2023. Before that, generally 10 years, or 20 years if the service member died on active duty.
This is separate from the Post-9/11 GI Bill and from transferred GI Bill entitlement. Compare them before choosing, because you may be eligible for more than one.

title: Specially Adapted Housing and Special Home Adaptation grants
summary: Grant money to buy, build, or modify a home so you can live in it with a service-connected disability. You can draw on the grant up to six separate times over your lifetime.
amount: Up to $126,526 (SAH) or $25,349 (SHA) in FY2026, usable across 6 lifetime uses
eligibility: You own or will own the home
SAH: qualifying service-connected disabilities include the loss, or loss of use, of more than one limb, and blindness in both eyes within set limits
SHA: qualifying disabilities include the loss, or loss of use, of both hands, and severe burn or respiratory injuries
details: Both grants cover buying, building, or adapting a permanent home to suit the disability.

FY2026 maximums, effective 1 October 2025: $126,526 for a Specially Adapted Housing grant under 38 U.S.C. 2101(a), and $25,349 for a Special Home Adaptation grant under 2101(b). Both rose 3.87 percent on the year.
Temporary Residence Adaptation, for adapting a home you are living in temporarily, is capped separately at $50,961 under 2101(a) or $9,099 under 2101(b) for FY2026.
You do not have to spend it all at once. You can use part in one year and the remainder later, up to six uses in total.
These figures change every 1 October with the cost-of-construction index, so check the current year before you plan around them.
